title: When is a linear optimal power flow safe to dispatch from, and which cheap AC repair makes it safe?
lede: research programme on linear OPF dispatch feasibility on the PGLib-OPF benchmark: the DC dispatch overloads branches on all 11 congested cases; a trust-region successive linearisation of the AC power flow repairs 7 of 11 at the AC optimum's cost, and on 12 held-out angle-limited (SAD) cases the same rules with linearised angle rows repair 7 of 11 (angle-blind: 3); at the AC optimum's voltage schedule (an oracle). Without it, at the case file's 1.0 pu setpoints, the repair clears 2 of 11 API and 2 of 11 SAD cases and none meets voltage and Q limits; a repair that moves voltage setpoints with P, with a small margin inside every limit, is fully feasible on 28 of 34 cases from that start at 0.17 to 0.34 % mean cost above the AC optimum (tuned on those cases; held-out test next); analytic Jacobian sensitivities give the same counts (29 of 34) with 2 power flows per round, but the QP, not the power flows, sets the run time
summary: An open research programme (opened 2026-11-12, track 21) on whether the dispatch from a linear optimal power flow, the model markets clear energy with, is feasible once the AC physics is applied, and how many AC power flows a repair needs to make it so at the AC optimum's cost. Benchmark: PGLib-OPF v23.07 (typical, congested API and small-angle-difference SAD sets of 12 cases, 14 to 300 buses), solved with PYPOWER, whose AC optima match the library's published values within 0.005 %. So far (experiments in infra-dcopf): the plain DC dispatch overloads branches on all 11 API cases with an AC optimum; a trust-region successive linearisation (finite-difference loss factors and flow sensitivities, a QP, an elastic l1 fallback) repairs 7 of 11 at the optimum's cost, with rules set on those cases; on the 12 SAD cases, held out, the same rules plus linearised angle-difference rows repair 7 of the 11 with an AC optimum, while the angle-blind version repairs 3 and lands 6.5–17.6 % below the optimum's cost by breaking up to 16 angle limits. Milestone 3 (2026-11-12): without that oracle schedule, at PGLib's own 1.0 pu setpoints, the same repair clears thermal, slack and angle limits on 2 of 11 API and 2 of 11 SAD cases (6 and 7 with it), none of its dispatches meets voltage and Q limits, and an AC OPF over voltages only after it makes 16 of 34 cases fully feasible at a mean 0.8–4.3 % above the optimum's cost. Milestone 3b (2026-11-12): a successive linearisation over P and the generator voltage setpoints, with voltage and Q limits as linear rows, is fully feasible on only 5 of 34 cases as pre-registered (it stops within 0.1 % of the limits on 19); with a small margin inside every limit (a variant chosen after that result) it is fully feasible on 18 of 34, and on 28 of 34 with the voltage-only stage after it, at a mean 0.17–0.34 % above the AC optimum's cost; not yet tested on held-out cases. Milestone 2 (2026-11-13): the same sensitivities from the power-flow Jacobian (one sparse solve per round, matching central differences to 1.3×10−5) give 19 and 29 of 34, so the counts do not hang on finite-difference noise; the run time falls only 1.1× because the QP takes 98–99 % of it, and a finished repair's cost moves by up to 3.1 points with the derivative source, since the method stops at its first feasible round. Limits: one AC solver, one load point per case, no baseline yet from LPAC or optimised linearisations. Target: IEEE Transactions on Power Systems.
